Consider what happens when a student lea: Consider what happens when a student leader submits a capstone report; that single event concerns the project, the team, three students, the guide who will, in practice, confirm it and the report version being submitted. A process-mining tool, however, needs to know which one of these is the case.
This question motivates the project. Cla: The project is motivated by this question. Against this backdrop, classic process mining starts from an event log in which every event has a case identifier, an activity name and a timestamp; the methods built on top of it (discovery, conformance checking, bottleneck analysis) assume that each event belongs to exactly one case.
If the project is chosen as the case, ea: If the project is chosen as the case, each project's history stays together, but the guide's workload across all projects disappears; if the student is chosen, the same submission appears three times, once per team member. One useful comparison is a group photograph. A flat view cuts one person out of the picture, and every person can be cut out in turn, but the resulting set of cut-outs no longer reveals who was standing next to whom.
The literature names these distortions. When one event is copied into several cases, the result is //convergence//, and when repeated events that belong to different objects of another type are merged into one case, the result is //divergence// [1]. Events that have no object of the chosen type are dropped from the flat log altogether, which is called //deficiency//.
Object-centric event logs avoid this cho: Object-centric event logs avoid this choice. One event can refer to any number of objects, each with a type, and objects can also be linked to each other. OCEL 2.0 [2] standardises this structure, with JSON, XML and SQLite formats, a qualifier on every link, and object attributes that can change over time.
Several studies show why this structure: Several studies reveal why this structure matters. Keeping the object graph improves machine-learning tasks on process data in comparison to flattened features [3], and Adams and van der Aalst [4] tackle convergence, divergence and deficiency together. In parallel, one-to-many links yielded false directly-follows relations in a food-company case study [5], and object-centric data has quality problems of its own [6]. In education, Miri et al. [7] converted Moodle activity into OCEL and found that group and resource links remain invisible in a student-centric log.
What we could not find was a study that: What we could not find was a study that measures these effects across several real logs. The problem is generally acknowledged; nonetheless, its size has not been reported. Suitable public data does exist: the Open University Learning Analytics Dataset (OULAD) [8] covers students, courses and assessments, and CROP [9] links Gerrit code reviews to code changes, a process closely related to report review.
A capstone has the same structure. Hassa: A capstone has the same structure. Hassani et al. [10] describe a department supervising more than 250 final-year computing projects, and Premchaiswadi and Porouhan [11] mined an online peer-review process and found bottlenecks and rule violations in reviewer handling. The Educational Capstone Portal, whose architecture is documented in our project repository, handles registration, team formation, report compilation, three review stages, faculty decisions and scoring; it writes an audit-log row for every state change. Its process is therefore strongly object-centric.
We set out to study that process directl: We set out to study that process directly, yet portal logs could not be obtained, and no public capstone or thesis-management event log was found. We therefore narrowed what we claim: the capstone is offered as a documented OCEL 2.0 design, and the measurements are made on seven real public logs [16]. This report keeps the two parts clearly separate.
First, flattening happens without notice: First, flattening happens without notice. Tools apply it by default and rarely report how many events were copied, dropped or merged.
Second, the evidence is thin. Convergenc: Second, the evidence is thin. Convergence and divergence are ordinarily explained with small examples or a single case study, and we found no work that reports how often and how strongly they occur across several real logs.
Third, capstones are coordination work. The questions that matter in practice (whether one guide is overloaded, or which team resubmits repeatedly) cut across cases, so a case-centric view does not fit them.
Fourth, our claims are limited to the da: Fourth, our claims are restricted to the data we can access. Portal data is not available to us, so a re-runnable measurement on public logs is the strongest evidence we can offer.
Table 1.1 states what the project covers: Table 1.1 states what the project covers and what it does not, so that its limits are clear from the start.
Two further points apply. A rule-based e: Two further points apply. A rule-based engine from our earlier work is kept at appendix level, since eleven rules on two logs cannot support a conclusion. In addition, a Moodle log from the University of Cádiz was downloaded as an eighth source but is not used in any result.

On the flattening problem itself, van de: On the flattening problem itself, van der Aalst [1] explained why one-case-per-event logs misrepresent processes with several interacting entities, and Adams and van der Aalst [4] went on to cover convergence, divergence and deficiency together. Both papers are conceptual, and neither reports how often these effects take place in real data.
OCEL 2.0 [2] is the format we build on; it stores events, objects, event-to-object (E2O) links and object-to-object (O2O) links, each with qualifiers, in JSON, XML or SQLite. Our own converters write the SQLite form, and we read the JSON and XML forms of the public logs.
On consequences, Waibel et al. [5] used: On consequences, Waibel et al. [5] applied a causal event graph to reveal that one-to-many links yield false directly-follows edges, but only on one company's data. Kabierski et al. In education, Miri et al. [7] is the clo: In education, Miri et al. [7] is the closest related work, since they applied object-centric mining to Moodle data; this project is therefore not the first use of OCEL in education. Premchaiswadi and Porouhan [11] mined an online peer-review process with a single case notion, and Hassani et al. [10] outline how a department supervises many final-year projects, with no event data.
Taken together, the reviewed work leaves: Taken together, the reviewed work leaves three gaps.
First, flattening problems are named but: First, flattening problems are named but not measured: convergence and divergence appear in small or single-case examples, and most of the object-centric evidence we found uses simulated logs.
Second, work on education and capstones: Second, work on education and capstones relies on learning-platform data, since object-centric educational mining uses Moodle activity. A review lifecycle with submit, review, reject, resubmit and score has no public object-centric dataset.
Third, capstone portal logs are not avai: Third, capstone portal logs are not available. Searches of Zenodo, 4TU and the web found no public capstone or thesis-management event log, so we cannot test the capstone claim directly.
Our approach is therefore to measure fla: Our strategy is therefore to measure flattening on real review-like and multi-entity logs, to give the capstone an OCEL 2.0 model, and to state the limits explicitly.

This section describes the model we desi: This section outlines the model we designed for the portal; it is a design, not a result. We derived it from the portal's documentation (the audit-trail, submission-system and scoring-system documents in the repository), and because no portal data is available, it has not been populated with portal data.
The portal writes an audit-log row for e: The portal writes an audit-log row for every state transition, and the documented action vocabulary gives eight event types: `PROJECT_CREATED`, `COMPILATION_STARTED`, `COMPILATION_SUCCESS`, `COMPILATION_FAILED`, `STUDENT_SUBMITTED`, `FACULTY_STARTED_VERIFICATION`, `FACULTY_ACCEPTED` and `FACULTY_REJECTED`. Each row carries a project identifier, the acting student or faculty member and a timestamp. In the model, an event relates to its project, to the acting student or faculty member, and, through joins on the project, to the team, the report version and the stage.
The model is shaped by a few documented facts. A score is written once and then locked. A rejection uses up one of three attempts and increments the report version, while compilation failures are free retries and do not use an attempt. The documentation lists the automatic move from stage R1 to R2 to R3 as a known gap, so the stage relation is part of the design, yet the current system does not fully populate it.
There are seven modules, M1 to M7. Each: There are seven modules, M1 to M7. Each one is a small Python script in the `realdata/src` directory, each reads what the one before it wrote, and Figure 4.1 shows how they connect.
fetch_sources.py reads a manifest (sourc: `fetch_sources.py` reads a manifest (`sources.json`) that lists each source with its record number, licence and expected files. For a Zenodo record it asks Zenodo for the file list, downloads each file, and compares the size and MD5 checksum with the record; a mismatch deletes the file and stops the run. OULAD comes from the UCI mirror and has no published checksum, so there we cap the download size and record the SHA-256. Every file gets a SHA-256 in a `SOURCE.md` next to it. If a download stalls, the script resumes from the partial file with an HTTP Range request; this was needed once during the study.
extract_archives.py unpacks each archive: `extract_archives.py` unpacks each archive into a new, empty directory next to it, and it refuses any archive with an absolute path or a parent-relative (`..`) member path.
Table 5.1 lists the sources, and Table 7: Table 5.1 lists the sources, and Table 7.1 gives the sizes of the logs.
Five logs already come in an OCEL format: Five logs already come in an OCEL format: Angular and Bundestag as JSON, Age of Empires as SQLite, Enron and Ethereum as parquet bundles. For the other two, `convert_crop.py` and `convert_oulad.py` build OCEL 2.0 SQLite files. CROP becomes three object types (change, person, project) with events like upload, comment, approve, merge and abandon, and OULAD becomes four (student, enrollment, presentation, assessment) with events like register, submit and unregister.
ocel_io.py loads every format into the s: `ocel_io.py` loads every format into the same four pandas tables. It hashes personal identifiers with a salted hash (the Enron e-mail addresses and the CROP names), splits the Enron e-mail address type by role (sender, recipient, copied) so each role can be a case notion, and for Ethereum cuts a contiguous window of 300,000 events. The flattening function used throughout the study is also defined there.
A case notion is an object type we choos: A //case notion// is an object type we choose as the case. Flattening on type //T// gives one row for every distinct pair of an event and a T-object, equivalent to the flattening function in `pm4py`; events with several T-objects are repeated, events with none are dropped, and only event-level attributes survive. A case notion counts as //analysed// when it covers at least 1,000 events, which leaves 38 case notions over the seven logs. Table 5.2 defines the metrics.
The thresholds (95% exclusivity, fan-out: The thresholds (95% exclusivity, fan-out of 1.5, 1,000 events) are our own choices. They sit at the top of `distortion.py` and `consequence.py`, and none of them was tuned to improve a result.
Distortion metrics tell us how much a fl: Distortion metrics tell us how much a flat view differs; the consequence analysis asks what an analyst would read differently. The reference is the object-centric view: every event counted once, plus the object-centric directly-follows relation, which is the union of consecutive-event pairs over the lifecycle of every object of every type. For each case notion we compare four outputs against that reference, and then we look at the process model an analyst would discover from the flat log.
C1, activity ranking: Spearman rank corr: C1, activity ranking: Spearman rank correlation of the flat activity counts with (a) the counts of the whole process, each event once, and (b) the counts of the same covered events each counted once, which isolates the effect of duplication. We also report the share of activities visible at all.
C2, directly-follows edges: duplication: C2, directly-follows edges: duplication of event pairs (flat pairs divided by distinct pairs), rank agreement of edge frequencies with and without duplicates, the largest inflation among the ten most frequent reference edges, and, when nested children exist, the share of flat edge instances whose edge type never occurs inside any child (the spurious edge mass).
C3, variants: distinct activity sequence: C3, variants: distinct activity sequences, variants per case, and the share of cases covered by the ten most frequent variants.
C4, entity ranking: for every other obje: C4, entity ranking: for every other object type with at least 30 objects, the rank correlation between the true number of events per object and the row count that a denormalised flat export of T would give, over the objects that appear in the export at all.
C5, discovered model: the Inductive Mine: C5, discovered model: the Inductive Miner with infrequent-behaviour filtering [12] (noise threshold 0.2, as implemented in `pm4py` [15]) runs on each flat log. The model is scored on the same flat log with token-based replay fitness [13] and token-based precision [14], and we record the size of the process tree, its //loop share// (the share of its visible activities that sit under a loop operator) and the share of the process's activities that the model contains at all.
Precision replays every prefix of every: Precision replays every prefix of every case, so its cost grows with the square of case length; we compute it only when the squared case lengths add up to at most 20 million, and each case notion gets an hour in total. The Inductive Miner copies its process tree with Python's `deepcopy` while simplifying it, and on cases of several thousand events that nests deeper than Python's default limit of 1,000 calls. Two Age of Empires II case notions failed on this account in our first runs, so `discovery.py` raises the limit inside the mining process.
Two details matter for fairness. Events: Two details matter for fairness. Events are coded by sorted event identifier, so ties in time always break the same way, and the analysis keeps //duplication// (the same event counted several times) apart from //narrowing// (events or activities a case notion never sees). An analyst can undo the first by de-duplicating on the event identifier; the second, however, cannot be recovered from a flat log.
Some object types would never be chosen: Some object types would never be chosen as a case notion. A farm in Age of Empires II, as an illustration, takes part in only a handful of activities. To separate this structural narrowing from narrowing that an analyst could plausibly encounter, we also look at the //widest// case notion of each log (the one covering the most events) and at //plausible// case notions, meaning those that cover at least half of the log's events. Both views were introduced after the first results were seen, so we report them over a range of thresholds rather than at 50% only.
Every number is computed on the full dat: Every number is computed on the full data, so the remaining uncertainty is about which events and which items happen to be in a log. `bootstrap.py` estimates it with 200 bootstrap replicates and a fixed seed. For counts of case notions it gives every event a Poisson(1) weight and recomputes coverage and visibility; for rank correlations it resamples the ranked items themselves (activities, or visible entities). An earlier version also applied event weights for the correlations and generated intervals that did not contain their own estimates: an entity with a single event receives the same weight in its true count and in its row count, which creates artificial agreement. The unweighted replicate reproduces every published value, and the script checks that before it starts.
We keep a rule-based engine from earlier: A rule-based engine is kept from earlier work, `cooc.py` with `registry.py`; it evaluates eleven natural rules (as an illustration, a change is merged only after an approval vote, or no submission after the assessment deadline) on native, flat and denormalised-flat views of CROP and OULAD. Two logs and eleven rules are too few to support a conclusion, so the engine is excluded from the main results.
sql_crosscheck.py re-implements four CRO: `sql_crosscheck.py` re-implements four CROP rules in plain SQL on the OCEL SQLite file, opened read-only. `check_consequence.py` compares the fast consequence code with a slow plain-Python version on a real slice of the Enron log, and `check_distortion.py` does the same for the distortion metrics, using only dictionaries and sets. By default it runs on 6,000-event slices of Enron, Bundestag and Age of Empires II; with `--full` (part of `make study`) it recomputes every metric on all seven full logs and compares the result with the published files. Finally, the OULAD counts are recomputed independently from the raw CSV files. Section 5.2 reports the results.
summarize_distortion.py, summarize_log_l: `summarize_distortion.py`, `summarize_log_level.py`, `summarize_consequence.py` and `summarize_discovery.py` combine the per-log JSON files into the CSV and Markdown tables used in Chapter 7. `make study` runs the main sequence and the full-log check, and `make extended` runs the bootstrap and the process-discovery comparison, which take much longer.

The logs cover code review, education, l: The logs cover code review, education, legislation, e-mail, blockchain and game play, which gives 38 analysed case notions. The Ethereum figures are for a contiguous window of 300,000 events from a log with 3.2 million.
The logs fall into three groups, shown i: The logs fall into three groups, laid out in Figure 7.1.
In the star logs (CROP and OULAD) every: In the star logs (CROP and OULAD) every event touches exactly one object of each type. Flattening copies nothing (1.00 copies per event) and, in the median, drops nothing; on these two measures the distortion is zero.
The partitioned logs (Bundestag, Age of: The partitioned logs (Bundestag, Age of Empires II, Ethereum) copy little, at most 1.27, 1.76 and 1.09 copies per event. Yet different object types cover different parts of the log, so the median case notion drops between 69% and 91% of the events.
In the fan-out logs (Angular commits and: In the fan-out logs (Angular commits and Enron) one event relates to many objects of the same type. The largest duplication is 81.65 copies per event in Angular (the branch case notion) and 2.11 in Enron.
Coupling adds a second perspective. Figu: Coupling adds a second perspective. Figure 7.2 shows the share of object-type pairs where the objects of one type are shared across the cases of the other. In every log except the Bundestag and Age of Empires, at least half the type pairs share more than half of their objects, and in Angular both of the two pairs do.
First, duplication alone rarely changes: First, duplication alone rarely changes a ranking. When the activity ranking from flat rows is compared with the ranking of the same events counted once, only 2 of the 38 case notions fall below a rank correlation of 0.95 (bootstrap interval 1 to 3): Angular files (0.81, interval 0.66 to 0.90) and the Enron "to" role (0.93). The Enron value is less certain: with only nine activities, its interval runs from 0.53 to 1.00. Where a log has no duplication, as in the star logs, the correlation is exactly 1.0.
Second, narrowing is the bigger effect. In 20 of the 38 case notions the flat log shows fewer than half of the activities of the whole process. The activity rank correlation with the whole process has a median of only 0.17 in the Bundestag (interval 0.14 to 0.29) and 0.21 in Age of Empires II (0.15 to 0.29). A flat view of those logs is therefore not a distorted picture of the whole process but a small part of it.
Much of this narrowing is structural. Ei: Much of this narrowing is structural. Eighteen of the 20 narrowed case notions come from the Bundestag and Age of Empires II, where an object type such as a written parliamentary question or a farm is in effect a sub-process of its own, and a farm cannot be expected to see the rest of the game. We therefore also inspected the case notions an analyst would plausibly choose. Fifteen of them cover at least half of their log, and 2 of those are still narrowed. Villager, in Age of Empires II, covers 52.8% of the events but shows 17% of the activities. OULAD's Assessment case notion covers 80% of the events and shows one activity in three: every submission is present, while every registration and withdrawal is lost. More importantly, two logs have no plausible case notion at all: the widest case notion covers 32.8% of the Bundestag events (and 3% of its 148 activities) and 37.4% of the Ethereum window. In the other five logs the widest case notion covers at least 95% of the events.
These counts do not depend on a single t: These counts do not depend on a single threshold. With the narrowing threshold at 0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6 and 0.7, the number of narrowed case notions is 17, 18, 20, 20 and 20. With the coverage threshold at 30% to 70%, there are 21, 16, 15, 13 and 13 plausible case notions, of which 5, 3, 2, 1 and 1 are narrowed, and OULAD Assessment is narrowed every time. Raising the 1,000-event cut-off to 2,000 or 5,000 leaves 15 of 33 and 10 of 28 narrowed, and in all 200 bootstrap replicates the counts remain at 20 narrowed, 15 plausible and 2 both.
Third, careless counting can mislead. Su: Third, careless counting can mislead. Suppose an analyst ranks entities (people, as an illustration) by counting rows in a denormalised flat export. Our initial expectation was that flatten: Our initial expectation was that flattening mainly duplicates events, and the data did not support this. Duplication is large in only two of the seven logs; the common pattern is that a case notion sees only part of the process, and the flat log gives no indication of what is missing. The usual quality check does not reveal this either: a model discovered from a narrowed flat log still replays that log almost perfectly, so fitness remains high precisely when the view is most partial.
For the capstone, only a hypothesis can: For the capstone, only a hypothesis can be stated, since no portal data is available. The portal's documented audit log relates each action to one project and to the person who acted. If real data has that shape, flattening on the project would copy few events, but it would hide how one guide's reviews spread across many projects, and it would hide the people; that is the narrowing pattern, not the duplication pattern. The next step is to test this on a de-identified portal log; until then, no claim about the portal is made.

We set out to study capstone review proc: We set out to study capstone review processes with OCEL 2.0. Portal logs were not available, so the project turned into two things: a documented OCEL 2.0 design of the capstone lifecycle, and a measurement of the effects of flattening on seven real public logs. The main conclusions are as follows.
First, a reproducible and verified pipel: First, a reproducible and verified pipeline has been built; it downloads and verifies seven public logs, converts two of them to OCEL 2.0, computes distortion metrics for 38 case notions and compares standard outputs between flat and object-centric views. A second, plain-Python implementation reproduces the distortion metrics exactly on all seven full logs, other independent checks agree with the parts they cover, and the checks caught three bugs of our own, which we fixed.
Second, flattening does not mainly dupli: Second, flattening does not mainly duplicate events. Duplication is large only in the fan-out logs, up to 81.65 copies of an event in Angular, and only 2 of 38 case notions fall below a rank correlation of 0.95 on account of duplication alone.
Third, the larger effect is narrowing. I: Third, the larger effect is narrowing. In 20 of 38 case notions the flat log shows fewer than half of the process's activities. Most of that comes from the structure of the logs; yet 2 of the 15 case notions that cover at least half of their log are narrowed too, and in two logs no case notion covers half of the events. The counts hold across every threshold we tried and in every bootstrap replicate.
Fourth, the usual quality checks do not: Fourth, the usual quality checks do not detect narrowing: a model discovered from a narrowed flat log still replays that log with a fitness of 0.955 or more, and divergence turns into loops that accept almost any order of events.
Fifth, careless counting from a flat exp: Fifth, careless counting from a flat export can be seriously misleading: worst-case entity rankings reach a rank correlation of 0.16 (Enron), -0.01 (Ethereum) and -0.41 (Age of Empires II), and none of the bootstrap intervals exceeds 0.2.
Sixth, the capstone model remains a desi: Sixth, the capstone model remains a design. We could not test it on portal data, and nothing is claimed about how real capstone teams behave.

Measuring Case-Notion Distortion and Its Consequences on Seven Real Object-Centric Event Logs//, which we submitted to the Journal of Intelligent Information Systems (Springer) in October 2026; it is under review.

The discovery comparison applies one miner, and the rule-based engine covers eleven rules on two logs, which we use for no conclusion.
